They have lives
outside your screen.

Gu Manning is decisive and guarded; Tang Tang is playful and expressive. Give them the same stress level and they should still feel like different people.

MOOD & NEEDS

Today isn't always the same.

Energy, stress, mood and social needs influence willingness to interact. A trusted friend may be offered quiet company where a stranger gets a brief reply.

AUTONOMOUS DAILY LIFE

The world keeps moving.

Residents work, eat, sleep, visit people and pursue interests. Their schedules respond to needs and personality. Meetings begin with introductions, not unearned familiarity.

RELATIONSHIPS & CONTINUITY

Getting closer changes things.

Familiarity, trust and shared experiences shape what they reveal. Messages, social posts and academy events provide other windows into their lives.

01 / The product

Your next task has
a place in the story.

Most task lists record what you do. Life OS explores how visible progress, a sense of place and relationships with fictional characters can make doing it feel more meaningful.

01 — ACT IN REAL LIFE

Bring your own ambitions.

Plan a study session, finish a project or build a habit. The goals remain yours; the product provides structure, focus tools and feedback.

02 — MAKE PROGRESS VISIBLE

See effort accumulate.

Completed actions contribute to growth dimensions, experience and an in-world economy. Academy ranks give that progress a longer-term direction.

03 — RETURN TO A LIVING WORLD

Have a reason to care.

Meet residents with their own routines, build relationships and follow unfolding events. The long-term design goal is for meaningful world unlocks to reward real action.

A navigable town brings eight growth directions and their residents into one setting.

Development screenshots from different iterations. Visuals, terminology and progression continue to evolve.

02 / Engineering the experience

More than a task list.
More than a dialogue tree.

The core challenge is consistency: a character’s location, mood, relationships and recent experiences need to tell the same story across every interaction.

State-driven simulation

Residents with their own routines

Schedules and changing needs inform where characters go and what they do. Personality differences influence their routines, rather than having everyone follow the player.

Context-aware interaction

The right line, at the right moment

Authored dialogue is selected using context such as time of day, emotional state, relationship history and whether the characters have actually met. Recent repetition is suppressed.

Shared state & persistence

Continuity across systems

Dialogue, events, messages and character activity draw on persistent world and relationship state. The prototype includes local browser saves; account-based cloud access is a later deployment step.

Iterative product development

Test the journey, not just the feature

Testing focuses on situations where systems collide: conversations during schedule changes, first meetings away from a character’s usual venue, and invitations while another activity is in progress.

Real-world action→Growth & rewards→World & relationship state→Contextual feedback

NPC behaviour uses rules and authored content. It does not depend on a live language-model call for every conversation.

03 / Commercial thesis

Build a useful tool.
Give it an emotional
reason to stay.

The opportunity is to combine the recurring usefulness of a productivity product with the attachment and self-expression of a narrative game.

What the next beta needs to proveFirst meaningful task completion · Repeat use across the first week · Whether the world strengthens the task habit · Interest in optional cosmetic and story purchases

A specific starting audience

Students and young professionals who enjoy cosy or character-driven games, but find conventional productivity tools emotionally flat.

A testable retention hypothesis

Visible progress creates immediate feedback; character attachment and ongoing world events offer a reason to return. The key question is whether those returns translate into real-world action.

Optional purchases, earned progression

A freemium model could pair a useful task-and-focus core with optional outfits, room styles, scene collections and story expansions. Core growth should come from action, not buying a higher rank.

Founder-led distribution

Development stories and product demonstrations on Xiaohongshu can attract early adopters, surface user feedback and build a community before a wider launch.

These are business hypotheses for validation, not claims of established revenue, retention or product–market fit.

04 / The builder

From a personal
idea to a product.

I’m Lea, a Computer Science student at UCL. Role-playing games made me wonder: what if the satisfaction of growing a character could help us make progress in our actual lives?

I’m building Life OS as an independent project, owning the product concept, world and interaction design, development priorities and hands-on testing. I use AI-assisted coding to implement and iterate, with a focus on making the systems work coherently together.

Current stage: a working browser prototype in active development. The next milestones are validating the action-to-world progression loop and preparing a small account-based beta. The linked playable build is an isolated demonstration, not a public launch of player accounts or cloud saves.
